title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery

Title:PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

report.summary: PharmAgents2 pairs extracted scientific decision skills with self-scaling parallel agents to run end-to-end drug discovery, yielding experimentally validated hits across three real-world studies.
report.background: Drug discovery remains one of the most expensive and failure-prone R&D pipelines in existence, with timelines routinely stretching past a decade and attrition rates above 90% in clinical stages. Over the past few years, AI has chipped away at individual stages — protein structure prediction, virtual screening, ADMET modelling, retrosynthesis — but each tool still requires a human to decide what to run next. The arrival of LLM-based scientific agents (Coscientist, ChemCrow, and various 'AI scientist' systems) shifted attention from single models to autonomous decision loops. Yet these agents typically explore narrowly, inherit little context across experiments, and are judged on final answers rather than the quality of their reasoning process. PharmAgents2 addresses exactly those three gaps: transferable decision knowledge, scalable parallel exploration, and process-level evaluation. Its 'virtual pharmaceutical company' framing signals a broader ambition — not a helper tool for chemists, but an autonomous organisation that proposes, prioritises and validates its own research programmes.
key_points: Paper2Skill mines public scientific literature and databases to extract reusable decision-making knowledge — not just facts, but judgements about which experiments to run and why. Combined with hand-built expert skills, this gives the agent a curated playbook for navigating the vast research space instead of reasoning from scratch at every step.

Self-Scaling Discovery spawns parallel agents that each inherit the accumulated research context and decision capabilities. Exploration therefore branches simultaneously across targets, hypotheses and discovery strategies, letting the system cover far more ground than a single linear agent chain while keeping each branch scientifically coherent.

The team built PharmAgents-Bench v0.1: 121 questions spanning nine decision scenarios plus three end-to-end tasks, scored against expert-defined process rubrics. This is notable because it grades the reasoning trajectory, not just the final answer — a harder and more meaningful test for autonomous science agents.

PharmAgents2 beat baselines in most decision categories and topped process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In real studies it proposed a previously unreported allosteric site on LpxH and found a novel inhibitor scaffold with confirmed activity, prioritised a covalent JAK1 strategy with validated compounds, and identified a new binding target for a known bioactive molecule.

The three real-world findings were subsequently confirmed by human-executed wet-lab experiments. That human-in-the-loop validation is what separates this from a pure benchmark result: the system's hypotheses survived contact with physical chemistry, which is the only test that ultimately matters in drug discovery.
report.impact: For the AI industry, PharmAgents2 reframes the agent debate from 'can models answer questions' to 'can agents run multi-month research programmes with auditable reasoning'. The process-rubric benchmark is arguably the more durable contribution — it gives the field a way to score decision quality, which will likely be adopted well beyond pharma. For developers, the architecture is a template: extract domain skills into an explicit knowledge layer, then scale exploration through context-inheriting parallel agents. Expect similar patterns to appear in materials science, synthetic biology and clinical trial design. For regular users, the practical signal is timeline compression — if autonomous systems can propose novel binding sites and scaffolds that survive experimental testing, the decade-long path from idea to candidate could shorten substantially, though regulatory and safety burdens remain entirely human. Near term, expect assistants rather than replacements.
report.tools: To follow up: PharmAgents and ChemCrow for agentic chemistry workflows; Coscientist for lab-automation agents; LangGraph, AutoGen or CrewAI for building context-inheriting multi-agent orchestrators; RDKit and ChEMBL for cheminformatics and bioactivity data; Boltz-2 or AlphaFold3 for structure and binding prediction; Dockstring or AutoDock-GPU for screening; and the PharmAgents-Bench rubric design as a model for building your own process-level evaluations.
